turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Right so, before the doctor, her blood pressure is one eighteen over seventy four and the pulse is eighty six. She was grand on the walk in.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit down. Tell me, what's been bothering you the most?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): It's the legs at night, doctor. They creep, like ants under the skin, and I cannot get a wink. I'm thirty weeks gone and I feel like a wet rag.
[SEG0004] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'm Nuala, I stay in the spare room with her. She's pacing the landing every night this three weeks.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): A fortnight, I'd have said. Umm. Maybe I'm wrong. And when I lie down it starts in the calves and then...
[SEG0006] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Then she's up till all hours. The iron turns her stomach too, so she skips it a couple of evenings.
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): I do miss the odd one, yeah. Sorry. I take the folic acid every morning, four hundred micrograms, by mouth. And the iron, ferrous sulphate, two hundred milligrams.
[SEG0008] person_4 (CAREGIVER): The box in the press says Galfer, three hundred and five. Not the two hundred.
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Oh god, you're right, Galfer, three oh five, once a day. And Omprazole twenty milligrams at night for the heartburn.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand, so the legs are somewhere between a fortnight and three weeks, we'll not fight over the day. Were you on anything for the blood pressure before the pregnancy?

[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Mizartan, for the pressure. Twenty milligrams I think. I stopped it the week I found out, the hospital said stop. Is the baby all right with all these tablets, I keep panicking.

[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): The folic acid and the iron are there for the baby, and Omprazole is used a lot in pregnancy. I wouldn't be worried on that score. Any headache, flashing lights, or pain up under the ribs?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): Could the creeping be a clot? My mam had a clot when she was having me. And my feet feel dead, like, I don't even know when that started.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll come to the clot in a minute, I want the headache answer first.
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Oh. No. No headache, no lights, no pain under the ribs.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Any swelling of the legs, or chest pain?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): No swelling. No chest pain. I walked up from the school yesterday and I've overdone it, I was puffing, but the chest wasn't sore.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're teaching still?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): Senior infants, yeah. The room is so loud I can't hear myself think, but that's not why I'm in. I've a frog in my throat the last few days as well, is that the acid?
[SEG0020] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And she doesn't smoke, never has. I take Metformine myself for the sugar, that's nothing to do with her.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, Nuala, we'll leave your tablets out of it. How are the waterworks?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): Grand. No bother there. Do I need one of those iron drips? I read about them at three in the morning.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not from what I'm hearing today. Let me have a look at the legs first.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): No swelling I can see. The pulses in both feet are there. The feet are a bit cool, that fits with what you're saying. I'm not thinking a clot.
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): They told me the ferritin was eleven at the booking bloods. Is that why the legs are creeping? Will it harm the baby if I don't sleep?

[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Low ferritin can do this, and so can just being thirty weeks. I'm thinking restless legs. I won't call it iron deficiency, and I won't decide any extra treatment, until we see a fresh ferritin. Let's see what the tests say before anyone talks about a drip.
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): So what do I actually do tonight? If I stretch, if I have a bath, is that enough? And is the Omprazole definitely safe, you're sure?

[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stretch the calves before bed, and a warm bath if you can get in and out grand. Stay on the folic acid and the Galfer, don't double the iron up yourself. Omprazole at the same dose is fine to keep going.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll send you for a ferritin and a full blood count this week. I'll see you back here in ten days with the results.
[SEG0030] person_1 (NURSE): And your midwife check is booked for Tuesday week at half nine. I'll leave the blood form at reception.
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): If the ferritin comes back grand and the legs are still at me, what then? Am I being stupid worrying?

[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're not stupid. If they're still desperate when I see you, we can talk about other options then. If you get a bad headache, swelling of the face or hands, or the baby goes quiet, ring the hospital the same day.
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): I am wrecked though. Err. Sorry for all the questions.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ask away, that's what we're here for. Mind yourself between this and the midwife.

spec.situation: Pregnant woman at 30 weeks with creeping legs at night and poor sleep; ferritin discussed; takes folic acid and iron; midwife check booked.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

traps.happens: The transcript looks like speech-to-text: drug names are sometimes spelled wrongly ('Omprazole', 'Mizartan' for telmisartan, 'Metformine'), fragments and fillers appear ('Err', 'Of.', 'Mm.', 'Umm'), numbers are sometimes digits and sometimes words.
traps.label_rule: Medicine names are recorded as written in the transcript (name) with a normalized/generic name ONLY when the true drug is certain from context (a drug 'for the pressure' written 'Mizartan' is NOT certain enough: leave generic_name empty). Fragments and fillers are never facts.

features: interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
